651.quote_or_event: “Truth is higher than everything; but higher still is truthful living.”
651.explanation: Guru Nanak ranks truthful conduct (sach aachaar) above everything, even above knowing the truth.
651.tie_back: The Kural says good allies bring increase, but goodness in the deeds themselves brings everything one could wish for; Guru Nanak likewise places the purity of one's own conduct above all else.
651.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 62, Siree Raag, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
651._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on the primacy of pure conduct; the Kural's contrast with good allies has no counterpart in this line.

652.quote_or_event: “Fareed, those deeds which do not bring merit - forget about those deeds.”
652.explanation: Sheikh Farid, whose saloks are included in the Guru Granth Sahib, tells the seeker simply to drop any action that yields no good.
652.tie_back: The Kural says one must always give up any deed that brings neither honour nor real good; Farid gives almost the same rule.
652.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1381, Salok Sheikh Farid (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
652._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one rule of renouncing fruitless deeds; Farid (a Sufi bhagat in the SGGS) measures merit spiritually and omits the Kural's concern for fame.

653.quote_or_event: “Those who have meditated on the Naam, the Name of the Lord, and departed after having worked by the sweat of their brows -O Nanak, their faces are radiant in the Court of the Lord, and many are saved along with them!”
653.explanation: The closing salok of Japji promises radiant faces to those whose lives combined remembrance of God with honest toil.
653.tie_back: The Kural tells those who would rise higher to avoid any deed that dims the light of their good name; Japji likewise links a shining face, a radiant honour, to a life of upright effort.
653.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8, Jap (Japji Sahib, closing salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
653._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: shares the image of radiance earned by right conduct, but frames it positively and in the divine court rather than as avoiding deeds that tarnish worldly reputation.

654.quote_or_event: Guru Tegh Bahadur, the ninth Guru, took up the cause of those facing forced conversion under Aurangzeb and, refusing to convert himself, was publicly beheaded in Delhi in 1675; Gurdwara Sis Ganj marks the place.
654.explanation: In the greatest personal danger the Guru chose death over an act he held to be dishonourable, and Sikhs remember him for that steadfastness.
654.tie_back: The Kural says people of clear understanding will not do anything shameful even in serious trouble; Guru Tegh Bahadur's refusal to renounce his faith at the cost of his life is a supreme Sikh example of that resolve.
654.source: The Pluralism Project, Harvard University, The Development of the Sikh Community
654._accuracy_note: Strong fit on refusing a disgraceful act under extreme pressure; martyrdom goes beyond the Kural's ordinary distress, and the source notes some details rest on Sikh tradition.

655.quote_or_event: “Acting in egotism, so very many have died. After making mistakes, they later repent and regret.”
655.explanation: Guru Nanak observes that deeds done from haumai (ego) end in regret and repentance afterwards.
655.tie_back: The Kural warns against doing anything that will later make one cry out in regret; Guru Nanak traces such regret to deeds done in egotism.
655.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 109, Raag Maajh, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
655._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: matches the theme of deeds that bring later regret, but does not give the Kural's second counsel of not repeating such a deed.

656.quote_or_event: “To take what rightfully belongs to another, is like a Muslim eating pork, or a Hindu eating beef.”
656.explanation: Guru Nanak makes taking another's due (hak paraaia) as abhorrent as the strongest taboo of each community, a line no circumstance excuses.
656.tie_back: The Kural says one must not do what the wise condemn even if it means watching one's own mother go hungry; Guru Nanak likewise treats wrongful gain as absolutely forbidden.
656.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 141, Raag Maajh (Majh ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
656._accuracy_note: Reasonable but partial: shares the absolute ban on wrongful gain, but does not take up the Kural's hardest case of a starving mother; Sikh ethics also strongly values care of family.

657.quote_or_event: At Saiyidpur (Eminabad), Macauliffe relates, Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo, a poor carpenter, and declined the feast of the rich steward Malik Bhago. Called to explain, he squeezed Lalo's coarse bread and Bhago's rich bread: milk flowed from the first and blood from the second, showing honest labour against wealth won by bribery and oppression.
657.explanation: The story contrasts the pure food of honest work (kirat karni) with the tainted riches of exploitation, and the Guru openly chose the poor man's bread.
657.tie_back: The Kural says the deepest poverty of good people is better than wealth gained through disgrace; the Guru's preference for Lalo's simple bread over Bhago's feast makes the same choice.
657.source: Max Arthur Macauliffe, The Sikh Religion, vol. 1 (1909), Life of Guru Nanak, ch. IV, pp. 43-44
657._accuracy_note: Strong, near-direct parallel (honest poverty over tainted wealth), though the miracle of milk and blood belongs to the hagiographic Janamsakhi tradition.

658.quote_or_event: “Why do you do such evil deeds, that you shall have to suffer so?”
658.explanation: This pauri of Asa ki Vaar warns that a person must reap the fruit of what they do, so wrong deeds only lead to their own suffering.
658.tie_back: The Kural says deeds the wise forbid bring suffering even when they succeed; the pauri likewise insists that wrong deeds return as suffering to their doer.
658.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 474, Raag Aasaa (Asa ki Vaar, Pauri 21) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
658._accuracy_note: Strong fit on wrong deeds rebounding as suffering; the Kural's point that suffering comes even after apparent success is implied, not stated. Asa ki Vaar's pauris are traditionally Guru Nanak's, though BaniDB tags this one to Guru Angad, so the author is not named.

659.quote_or_event: “It was not gathered without sin, and it does not go along with the dead.”
659.explanation: In his hymns on Babur's invasion Guru Nanak looks at the riches the defeated rulers lost and says that such wealth is gathered only through sin and departs from its owners in the end.
659.tie_back: The Kural says whatever is taken by making others weep will leave its taker weeping; Guru Nanak watched wealth gained by oppression being stripped from its holders amid lament.
659.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 417, Raag Aasaa, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
659._accuracy_note: Strong thematic fit on ill-gotten wealth that departs; the Kural's second line, that honestly gained wealth returns, is not in this verse.

660.quote_or_event: “Falsehood will come to an end, O Nanak, and Truth will prevail in the end.”
660.explanation: Guru Nanak teaches that whatever rests on falsehood runs out, and only what rests on truth endures.
660.tie_back: The Kural compares securing oneself with wealth gained by deceit to storing water in an unbaked clay pot; Guru Nanak likewise says that what is built on falsehood cannot last.
660.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 953, Raag Raamkalee (Ramkali ki Vaar, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
660._accuracy_note: Reasonable fit on the impermanence of what deceit builds; the line is general and lacks the Kural's specific image of the unbaked pot and its focus on statecraft.
